title: Multi-Tenant RAG Documents API
tagline: A question-answering service where separate teams upload their own documents and query only their own.
result: Fully self-hosted: chunking, embedding, retrieval and generation all run on the host, so tenant documents never leave the machine.
problem: Teams sit on piles of internal documents they cannot search by meaning, and pasting them into a hosted chat tool moves private material off-premise. Most retrieval examples assume one corpus and one user, so two teams sharing an instance would read each other's files.
architecture: `/ingest` takes a document and a namespace, splits the text into overlapping chunks so a passage spanning a boundary stays retrievable, embeds each chunk with a local Ollama model, and writes the vectors into ChromaDB scoped to that namespace. `/ask` embeds the question, retrieves the closest chunks within a single namespace, and hands them plus the session's recent turns to the local generation model.

Namespace is required on both paths, so a cross-tenant read is not a permission check that can be misconfigured; it is a query that cannot be expressed. Chunking and retrieval are deterministic Python and the model is called only twice, to embed and to answer, so a wrong answer stays traceable to the chunks it cited.

diagram.caption: Both model calls stay local; the namespace narrows retrieval before generation.

decisions.because: one warm index instead of many, and isolation becomes a property of the query rather than a setting someone can get wrong.
no per-token cost and no document leaves the host, accepting slower generation and manual model management.
duplicated tokens in the index, but answers stop being cut off at paragraph boundaries.
follow-ups work with no schema to maintain, at the cost of losing history on restart.

impact: Stateless retrieval endpoints became a usable conversation: upload over HTTP, then ask follow-ups in the bundled interface without restating context. The isolation model is the reusable part, the problem row-level security solves in a relational database, handled at the vector layer and skipped by most retrieval examples. Every namespace lists its chunks, so a wrong answer stays traceable.

out_of_scope: No auth on either endpoint, since the target was one trusted deploy.
Sessions live in memory, so it runs on a single node.
